intro.title: Reading CSV data
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Most data arrives as a file, and the most common kind is **CSV**: comma-separated values. It is plain text, one row per line, with commas between the values and the column names on the first line:

```
member,book,days
Ana,The Long Walk,12
Ben,Seed Saving,20
Cy,River Birds,9
```

`read.csv()` turns that into a data frame. Normally you give it a file name, `read.csv("loans.csv")`. In CodeQuest there are no files to open, so the challenges give the text directly with `text =`, which works exactly the same way:

```
loans <- read.csv(text = "
member,book,days
Ana,The Long Walk,12
Ben,Seed Saving,20
Cy,River Birds,9
")
```

Always look at what you got with `str()` straight away. `read.csv()` guesses each column's type from its values: a column of numbers becomes numeric, but if even one value isn't a number (`"N/A"`, `"12 days"`, `"$3.40"`), the whole column comes in as text. Spotting that early saves a lot of confusion.

Useful arguments: `na.strings = c("", "N/A")` tells R which texts mean "missing", and `strip.white = TRUE` removes stray spaces around values. Writing is the mirror image: `write.csv(df, "clean.csv", row.names = FALSE)`.

In many countries spreadsheets save "CSV" with `;` between the values and `,` as the decimal point (`2,50`). `read.csv2()` reads that style; it is `read.csv()` with those two settings changed.

The rest of this quest is about the cleaning that usually comes next.

intro.title: Fixing column names
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Column names in real files are written for people: `Member Name`, `E-mail`, `Age (years)`. R needs names it can use after `$`, so `read.csv()` quietly changes them, turning every space and symbol into a dot:

```
members <- read.csv(text = "
Member Name,E-mail,Age (years),Joined On
Ana Silva,ana@example.org,34,2026-09-01
Ben Okafor,ben@example.org,41,2026-09-03
")
names(members)   # "Member.Name" "E.mail" "Age..years." "Joined.On"
```

Those work, but they are awkward to type and easy to get wrong. A good habit is to tidy all the names at the start: small letters, words joined with `_`, no symbols. Assign new names with `names()`:

```
names(members) <- c("name", "email", "age", "joined")
```

For many columns, clean them with text tools instead of typing every name: `tolower()`, then `gsub()` to turn runs of dots into `_` and trim `_` from the ends.

```
n <- tolower(names(members))
n <- gsub("\\.+", "_", n)      # one or more dots become _
n <- gsub("^_|_$", "", n)       # no _ at the start or end
```

To rename just one column, assign to that position: `names(members)[3] <- "age"`, or find it by name: `names(members)[names(members) == "E.mail"] <- "email"`.

intro.title: Numbers stored as text
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A very common problem: a column that should be numbers came in as text because of extra characters. A currency sign, a thousands comma, a unit, a space:

```
price <- c("$3.40", "$12.00", "$1,250.50", " $8 ")
as.numeric(price)    # all NA, with a warning
```

The fix is to remove the extra characters with `gsub()`, then convert. Use `fixed = TRUE` when the character to remove has a special meaning in patterns, like `$` (which means "end of text") or `.`:

```
price <- gsub("$", "", price, fixed = TRUE)   # remove $
price <- gsub(",", "", price, fixed = TRUE)   # remove the thousands comma
price <- as.numeric(trimws(price))
```

After converting, **always check for new NAs**. `as.numeric()` turns anything it can't read into NA, so compare the number of NAs before and after: `sum(is.na(price))`. Any surprise NA is a value you haven't cleaned yet.

Units work the same way: `gsub(" kg", "", weights, fixed = TRUE)`. When a column mixes units, such as `"500 g"` and `"1.2 kg"`, split the cleaning: find the rows with each unit with `grepl()` and convert them separately.

To check a whole column at once: `suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))` gives NA for the values that still aren't numbers, and `x[is.na(that)]` shows you which they are.

intro.title: Cleaning text values
intro.bodyMarkdown:
When people type categories, the same answer arrives in many forms: `"Kale"`, `"kale "`, `"KALE"`, `" kale"`. To R these are four different values, so `table()` counts them separately and filters miss some of them.

```
crop <- c("Kale", "kale ", "KALE", "beans", " Beans")
table(crop)    # five different values
```

The standard fix is to trim the spaces and choose one case. Small letters are the usual choice:

```
crop <- tolower(trimws(crop))
table(crop)    # beans 2, kale 3
```

Runs of spaces inside the text need `gsub(" +", " ", x)`. Typos and spelling variants (`"courgette"`, `"courgettes"`, `"zucchini"`) don't follow a rule; look at `table()` or `sort(unique(x))` to find them, then fix them one by one, as in the next stage.

For proper names, small letters look wrong in a report. A neat way to capitalise each word is `tools::toTitleCase()`: `tools::toTitleCase("ana silva")` gives `"Ana Silva"`. The `tools::` part says which package the function comes from; it is part of every R installation.

Always check the result with `table()` or `unique()`: it is the quickest way to see that every variant has been caught.

intro.title: Recoding values
intro.bodyMarkdown:
**Recoding** means changing values to the ones you want: fixing variants, shortening codes into words, or merging categories. Three ways, from the simplest:

**One value:** assign to the matching positions: `crop[crop == "zucchini"] <- "courgettes"`.

**A few values at once:** `%in%` finds them all: `crop[crop %in% c("courgette", "zucchini")] <- "courgettes"`.

**A whole code list:** a **lookup** vector with names maps each code to its meaning. Indexing it by the codes gives the meanings, in order:

```
size_names <- c(S = "small", M = "medium", L = "large")
sizes <- c("M", "S", "M", "L")
unname(size_names[sizes])    # "medium" "small" "medium" "large"
```

A code missing from the lookup becomes `NA`, which is useful: it shows you every code you didn't expect.

For yes/no style answers, `ifelse()` or `%in%` turns many forms into TRUE/FALSE: `answer %in% c("yes", "y", "1")`. And to merge categories, recode several into one, such as every leafy crop into `"greens"`.

intro.title: Duplicates
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Duplicates creep in when someone submits a form twice, when two files overlap, or when the same thing is entered by two people. They make counts and totals too big, so finding them is a standard cleaning step.

`duplicated()` is TRUE for every value (or row) that has **already appeared** earlier. The first copy is FALSE, later copies TRUE:

```
duplicated(c("a", "b", "a", "c", "a"))    # FALSE FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE
```

So `sum(duplicated(x))` counts the extra copies, and `x[!duplicated(x)]` keeps the first of each, which is what `unique(x)` does too.

On a data frame, `duplicated(df)` compares **whole rows**. Two rows are duplicates only if every column matches:

```
signups <- data.frame(
  email = c("ana@example.org", "ben@example.org", "ana@example.org", "cy@example.org", "ben@example.org"),
  workshop = c("compost", "compost", "compost", "seeds", "seeds")
)
duplicated(signups)          # FALSE FALSE TRUE FALSE FALSE
signups[!duplicated(signups), ]
```

Often, though, what defines a duplicate is a **key**: one person should appear once, whatever else differs. Then test that column alone: `signups[!duplicated(signups$email), ]` keeps each email's first row. Be sure that is what you want: here it would drop Ben's second, different workshop.

Before deleting anything, look at the duplicates: `signups[duplicated(signups$email) | duplicated(signups$email, fromLast = TRUE), ]` shows every row whose email appears more than once.

intro.title: Handling missing values
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Missing values hide in many disguises: an empty cell, `"N/A"`, `"-"`, `999`, `-1`. The first job is to make every one of them a real `NA`, so R knows. Then you choose what to do with them.

```
survey <- read.csv(text = "
visitor,age,rating,comment
1,34,5,Lovely
2,,4,
3,58,N/A,Too busy
4,-1,3,ok
5,27,,
6,41,5,Great
")
```

Here `age` has an empty value and a `-1` (a typing error, not an age), and `rating` has `"N/A"` and an empty value, which made it a text column. Fix the disguises:

```
survey$rating[survey$rating %in% c("", "N/A")] <- NA
survey$rating <- as.numeric(survey$rating)
survey$age[survey$age < 0] <- NA
```

Then decide, column by column, and write down what you did:

| Choice | How | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leave them | `na.rm = TRUE` in summaries | Usually the honest default |
| Drop rows | `df[!is.na(df$col), ]` | When that column is essential for the question |
| Fill in | `x[is.na(x)] <- median(x, na.rm = TRUE)` | Only with a good reason, and say so |

Filling in ("imputing") makes the data look complete, but the filled values are guesses. Filling with the median keeps the centre unchanged but makes the spread look smaller than it is. Always report how many values were missing.

intro.title: Dates from text
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Dates in files come in many shapes: `2026-10-30`, `30/10/2026`, `10/30/2026`, `30 Oct 2026`. `read.csv()` reads them all as text, so the first step is always `as.Date()` with the right `format`:

| Written as | format |
| --- | --- |
| `2026-10-30` | `"%Y-%m-%d"` (the default) |
| `30/10/2026` | `"%d/%m/%Y"` |
| `10/30/2026` | `"%m/%d/%Y"` |
| `30 Oct 2026` | `"%d %b %Y"` |
| `30.10.26` | `"%d.%m.%y"` (small y: two-digit year) |

A date that doesn't fit the format becomes `NA`. As with numbers, count the NAs after converting to find the ones that need attention.

Watch out for **day/month confusion**: `03/04/2026` is 3 April in most of the world and March 4 in the US. Look for a value with a day over 12 (like `30/10`) to tell which way round a file is.

Once they are real dates, you can pull out parts for grouping: `format(d, "%Y-%m")` gives the year and month, perfect for monthly totals with `tapply()`. `weekdays(d)` gives the day of the week.

```
d <- as.Date(c("02/09/2026", "15/09/2026", "03/10/2026"), format = "%d/%m/%Y")
format(d, "%Y-%m")    # "2026-09" "2026-09" "2026-10"
```

When a column mixes two formats, convert with each format and combine: where the first gives NA, use the second. `ifelse()` drops the Date type, so assign into the NAs instead: `d[is.na(d)] <- as.Date(x[is.na(d)], format = "%d/%m/%Y")`.

intro.title: Hard side quest: Sensor readings
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Two temperature sensors in the school greenhouse log a reading three times a day. When one fails it writes `-999` or `error`, or nothing at all, and sensor A once logged 61 °C on a cool autumn afternoon.

```
raw <- "time,sensor,temp
2026-10-28 08:00,A,18.2
2026-10-28 12:00,A,-999
2026-10-28 16:00,A,21.4
2026-10-28 08:00,B,error
2026-10-28 12:00,B,22.9
2026-10-28 16:00,B,23.5
2026-10-29 08:00,A,17.6
2026-10-29 12:00,A,20.8
2026-10-29 16:00,A,61.0
2026-10-29 08:00,B,17.9
2026-10-29 12:00,B,
2026-10-29 16:00,B,22.1"
```

Turn every failure into a real NA, remove the impossible value, and build a daily summary. The last challenge shows:

```text
2026-10-28: 4 readings, mean 21.5, max 23.5
2026-10-29: 4 readings, mean 19.6, max 22.1
```

challenges.title: Easy: Failures as NA
challenges.promptMarkdown: Read `raw` into `readings` so that empty values, `error` and `-999` all become NA, making `temp` numeric.

challenges.title: Medium: The day
challenges.promptMarkdown: Add a column `day`: the date part of `time`, as a real date.
challenges.hint: The first 10 characters are the date: `as.Date(substr(readings$time, 1, 10))`.

challenges.title: Medium: Impossible values
challenges.promptMarkdown: A greenhouse in October isn't over 50 °C. Make those temperatures NA.
challenges.hint: `readings$temp[readings$temp > 50] <- NA`. The NAs already there stay NA.

tests.label: temp now has 4 NAs and nothing over 50

challenges.title: Hard: Gaps per sensor
challenges.promptMarkdown: Make `gaps` the number of missing readings per sensor.

challenges.title: Hard: Daily means
challenges.promptMarkdown: Make `daily` the mean temperature per day, leaving out the NAs, rounded to 1 decimal place.

challenges.title: Expert: The daily report
challenges.promptMarkdown:
Show one line per day with the number of known readings, the mean (1 decimal place) and the maximum:

```text
2026-10-28: 4 readings, mean 21.5, max 23.5
2026-10-29: 4 readings, mean 19.6, max 22.1
```
challenges.hint: Loop over `unique(readings$day)` (use `as.character()` so the loop keeps the text), take that day's known temperatures, and `cat()` a line.
challenges.solution:
raw <- "time,sensor,temp
2026-10-28 08:00,A,18.2
2026-10-28 12:00,A,-999
2026-10-28 16:00,A,21.4
2026-10-28 08:00,B,error
2026-10-28 12:00,B,22.9
2026-10-28 16:00,B,23.5
2026-10-29 08:00,A,17.6
2026-10-29 12:00,A,20.8
2026-10-29 16:00,A,61.0
2026-10-29 08:00,B,17.9
2026-10-29 12:00,B,
2026-10-29 16:00,B,22.1"
readings <- read.csv(text = raw, na.strings = c("", "error", "-999"))
readings$day <- as.Date(substr(readings$time, 1, 10))
readings$temp[readings$temp > 50] <- NA
for (d in as.character(unique(readings$day))) {
  t <- readings$temp[readings$day == as.Date(d) & !is.na(readings$temp)]
  cat(d, ": ", length(t), " readings, mean ", round(mean(t), 1), ", max ", max(t), "\n", sep = "")
}
